This article applies `isoformic` to Oxford Nanopore long-read cDNA sequencing of 22Rv1 prostate cancer cells
treated with lorecivivint against vehicle-treated cells
[@vangoubergen2024; GEO [GSE259334](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE259334)].
Lorecivivint inhibits the CDC-like kinases (CLKs), which phosphorylate splicing factors.
Long reads often span a transcript from end to end,
so they assign reads to isoforms with less ambiguity than short reads.
The analysis is the same as for short reads.
Only the quantification step changes.

## The data

The 6 samples (3 vehicle, 3 lorecivivint) were quantified with Oarfish [@oarfish] in its nanopore cDNA mode.
The reference was the GENCODE v49 transcripts [@gencode], with 30 bootstrap replicates per sample.
Each sample has 6.3 to 7.0 million reads assigned to transcripts.
Transcripts were tested with `swish` [@swish] on the bootstrap replicates.
Genes were tested with `DESeq2` on the summed counts.
The scripts that download the reads from SRA and run every step are in `data-raw/case_studies/` of the package repository.

The result is an `IsoformicExperiment` saved with `write_isoformic()`.
It keeps the complete differential expression tables (every tested transcript and gene).
The expression assays and exon structures cover only a panel of 48 genes, so that the object fits in the repository.
It is not installed with the package.
`read_oarfish()` creates the same object from the Oarfish output directly,
as shown in the [preprocessing article](isoformic-preprocess.html).

```{r}
#| message: false
library(isoformic)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data_dir <- "data/prostate_ont"
iso <- read_isoformic(data_dir)
iso
col_data(iso)
iso@metadata[c("quantification", "transcript_de", "gene_de")]
```

## Checking the samples first

The first principal component of the gene-level counts does not separate the treatments, but the second one does.
With three samples per group there is no sign of a batch to adjust for.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
pca <- read_parquet(fs::path(data_dir, "sample_pca.parquet")) |>
  left_join(col_data(iso), by = "sample_id")
ggplot(pca, aes(PC1, PC2, color = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    x = sprintf("PC1 (%.0f%%)", 100 * pca$var_PC1[1]),
    y = sprintf("PC2 (%.0f%%)", 100 * pca$var_PC2[1])
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Differential expression at two levels

```{r}
deg <- de_gene(iso)
det <- de_tx(iso)
c(
  genes_tested = nrow(deg),
  genes_fdr_5 = sum(deg$qvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  transcripts_tested = nrow(det),
  transcripts_fdr_5 = sum(det$qvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
)
```

At a false discovery rate of 5%, `DESeq2` finds 140 genes and `swish` 287 transcripts.
`swish` computes its p-values from permutations of the samples.
Three against three samples allow only a few distinct permutations.
All 287 significant transcripts share the smallest q-value, so they are ranked by fold change below.

```{r}
range(det$qvalue[det$qvalue < 0.05], na.rm = TRUE)
```

Most significant transcripts are protein coding, followed by lncRNAs:

```{r}
det |>
  filter(qvalue < 0.05) |>
  left_join(tx_annot(iso), by = "transcript_id") |>
  count(transcript_type, sort = TRUE)
```

`isoform_switches()` relates the two levels.
It uses the default cutoffs of the experiment:
an absolute log2 fold change of at least 1 and a false discovery rate below 5%.
Two thirds of the genes with a significant transcript have no significant change of their total expression
(`det_not_deg`).

```{r}
switches <- isoform_switches(iso)
table(switches$switch_type)
switches |>
  filter(switch_type == "det_not_deg") |>
  select(gene_name, n_tx_tested, n_det_up, n_det_down, det_sig_types, gene_log2FC) |>
  head(10)
```

## The CLK genes regulate themselves

The CLK genes are among them: lorecivivint raises one protein coding isoform each of *CLK1*, *CLK3* and *CLK4*.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 10
plot_log2fc(iso, feature = c("CLK1", "CLK3", "CLK4"), ncol = 2)
```

The gene-level results show why the classification needs care.
*CLK1* and *CLK3* are significant in `DESeq2`, but their shrunken fold changes (1.8-fold) are below the 2-fold cutoff.
For that reason `isoform_switches()` does not count them as changed genes:

```{r}
deg |>
  left_join(annot_data_genes(iso)[c("gene_id", "gene_name")], by = "gene_id") |>
  filter(gene_name %in% c("CLK1", "CLK3", "CLK4")) |>
  select(gene_name, log2FC, qvalue, deg_sig)
```

The isoforms of *CLK1* explain most of its gene-level change.
`CLK1-201` encodes the full-length kinase.
`CLK1-204` is the same transcript without exon 4, which shifts the reading frame and makes it a target of
nonsense-mediated decay.
`CLK1-210` keeps the introns on both sides of exon 4.
CLK1 activity favours the skipping of its own exon 4,
and CLK inhibitors shift the balance towards the full-length isoform [@uzor2018].
The long reads show that shift.
The full-length isoform rises from about 17 to 46 transcripts per million.
The skipped one falls from about 4 to 1.5 (not significant on its own, with q = 0.25).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot_tx_expr(iso, gene_name = "CLK1", group = "condition")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10
plot_genomic_context(iso, gene_name = "CLK1")
```

## The genes of the original study

@vangoubergen2024 report that CLK inhibition lowers the expression of the androgen receptor splice variant ARV7
through the CLK2/SRSF9 axis.
In these three against three nanopore samples, no transcript of *AR*, *CLK2* or *SRSF9* reaches a false discovery
rate of 5%.
*SRSF3* has one protein coding isoform with a small but significant decrease.

```{r}
det |>
  left_join(tx_annot(iso), by = "transcript_id") |>
  filter(gene_name %in% c("AR", "CLK2", "SRSF9", "SRSF3")) |>
  summarise(
    n_tested = n(),
    best_qvalue = min(qvalue),
    log2FC_of_best = log2FC[which.min(qvalue)],
    .by = gene_name
  )
```

## Enrichment by transcript type

The package directory holds the hallmark gene sets of MSigDB [@msigdb].
`run_enrichment()` ranks the transcripts by fold change
and runs the enrichment separately for each group of transcript types.

```{r}
#| warning: false
genesets <- read_gmt(fs::path(data_dir, "genesets.gmt"))
set.seed(42)
enrichment <- run_enrichment(iso, genesets, pval_cutoff = 0.05)
table(enrichment$experiment)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10
plot_enrichment(enrichment, n = 20)
```

At an adjusted p-value below 0.05, three gene sets go down in the protein coding isoforms of the treated cells:
androgen response, cholesterol homeostasis and mitotic spindle.
This agrees with the anti-proliferative effect of lorecivivint reported by @vangoubergen2024.
The proliferation sets (G2M checkpoint, E2F and MYC targets) go down in the retained intron
and other unproductive isoforms.
They do not go down in the protein coding ones.
Only the transcript-level analysis shows this part of the response to the drug.
